study.title: Jeremiah 36 - The roll burned and the word that cannot be erased
study.overview: Jeremiah 36 shows a solemn attempt to call Judah to repentance by means of the written word. God sends Jeremiah to record his messages from the days of Josiah; Baruch writes and reads the roll publicly, first to the people, then to the princes and finally to King Jehoiakim. The reaction of the leaders reveals partial listening, human fear and, in the case of the king, open contempt: he cuts and burns the roll, but cannot destroy the word of God. The chapter ends with the renewed judgment against Jehoiakim and the order to rewrite the content, plus other similar words.

outline.title: God orders to register and announce the message
outline.explanation: The LORD commands Jeremiah to write down all that he has spoken against Israel, Judah, and the nations. The purpose is not only to inform, but to lead the house of Judah to listen, to convert and receive forgiveness. As Jeremiah is prevented from entering the house of the LORD, Baruch writes and reads the scroll in the temple, in the context of a fasting day, making the divine warning public.

outline.title: The message reaches the people and princes
outline.explanation: In the fifth year of Jehoiakim, during a proclaimed fast, Baruch reads the scroll in a reliance on the temple before the people. Micah hears, go down to the king's house and report everything to the princes. They call Baruch, ask him to read again, are alarmed and recognize the seriousness of the words, even advising Jeremiah and Baruch hiding.

outline.title: King rejects the word and destroys it
outline.explanation: The princes bear the scroll to Jehoiakim King, and Jeudi reads it before him. Instead of humbling, the king cuts the scroll and spears him to the fire, despising the requests of some princes so that he would not burn it. He still orders the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the text points out that the LORD had hidden them.

outline.title: God reiterates judgment and sends rewrite the scroll
outline.explanation: After the burning of the scroll, the LORD sends Jeremiah to take another and write again the same words. Jehoshakim receives a personal sentence: he will have no seed sat on the throne of David, and his body will be exposed to shame. The chapter ends with the punishment promised and with the expansion of the material, for many other similar words have been added.

study.context: The chapter is in the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah. The notes report that the fourth year of his reign was associated with a critical moment for Jerusalem, and that a fast was proclaimed the following year. The text highlights Baruch's role as a scribe and the practice of reading prophetic messages in public in the temple. The roll was a material writing format used to preserve and spread spoken words. All this serves God's purpose to warn the people before the judgment.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the word of God is persevering, public and effective, even when rejected by rulers. There is a strong call to repentance: the proclamation of judgment aims to awaken obedience and pave the way for forgiveness, not just produce fear. Also appears human responsibility before revelation: to hear, tremble, tear the heart or, on the contrary, to harden and resist. Jehoiakim represents the proud refusal to submit to the word; in contrast, Baruch faithfully serves as a scribe and reader. Theologically, the text shows that destroying the material support does not nullify the divine message, for the Lord makes it rewritten and confirms its verdict.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter highlights Jehoiakim's cynical response to God's effort to call him to repentance and obedience to the covenant; the situation is presented as morally desperate.
The scroll was prepared to gather, in written form, a summary of Jeremiah's messages, so that the people could remember what they had heard and understand it better at once.
The roll was to serve as a testimony for future generations, preserving God's warnings against Judah and the nations in a durable and public format.

questions: How do I react when the Word of God confronts my ways: with repentance or with resistance similar to that of Jehoiakim?
What does the text teach about the difference between hearing the message of God and actually submitting to it?
How can my life reflect Baruch's fidelity, which served the word without seeking prominence?
study.practice: Take time to listen to Scripture with humility and ask God to show specific areas of repentance. If you just receive warnings without changing, make a concrete answer today: confess a sin, interrupt a wrong practice and share the Word with someone else faithfully, without manipulating your message. The chapter also encourages to value records, readings, and biblical memorization as a means of preserving and transmitting the truth of God.
study.uncertainty: The given notes give approximate dates and historical readings on the fasting and the context of the reign, but do not allow to detail with absolute precision the chronology beyond what is already in the text and in the comments. It is also not possible to affirm with certainty, only by this material, how many times Baruque had already read the roll before the main public reading. Interpretations about the spiritual state of Jehoiakim and the exact reach of the "many other similar words" are legitimate but not detailed in the biblical text.
